value.overview: The Great Kiskadee (Pitangus sulphuratus) is a large, bold tyrant flycatcher recognized by its bright yellow underparts, brown back, black-and-white head pattern, and loud, distinctive call. It is one of the most adaptable flycatchers in the tropical Americas, using open woodland, riversides, gardens, farms, wetlands, and towns. Often conspicuous and aggressive, it catches insects from exposed perches but also eats fruit, small vertebrates, and aquatic prey.
value.classification: The Great Kiskadee belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, in the order Passeriformes. It is the only species in the genus Pitangus.
value.identification: This stocky flycatcher is about 22–25 cm long, with a large dark bill, brown upperparts, bright yellow breast and belly, and a long brown tail. Its head is strongly patterned: a black crown and broad black eye mask contrast with a white eyebrow, white throat, and white crown stripe. Rufous patches are visible in the wings during flight. Its piercing, emphatic call is commonly rendered as “kis-ka-dee.” It may resemble the smaller Social Flycatcher, but is noticeably larger and heavier-billed.
value.rangeHabitat: The Great Kiskadee ranges from southern Texas and Mexico through Central America and much of South America. In Costa Rica it is a widespread, common year-round resident, including both Caribbean and Pacific lowlands and many human-modified areas. It favors open or lightly wooded habitats near water, such as river edges, ponds, lakes, mangroves, pastures, forest clearings, gardens, parks, villages, and plantations. It generally avoids extensive, closed-canopy forest but can occur near forest margins and disturbed areas.
value.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the Great Kiskadee is generally resident rather than migratory and may be seen throughout the year. Individuals can make local movements in response to food, water, breeding, or habitat conditions, but the species is not considered a regular long-distance migrant there.
value.breeding: Great Kiskadees are typically monogamous and defend breeding territories, often noisily. Both adults build a bulky, domed nest with a side entrance using grasses, twigs, fibers, and sometimes human-made materials. Nests may be placed in trees, shrubs, cavities, or on structures, often in exposed positions. A clutch usually contains three or four eggs. The female generally performs most incubation, while both parents feed the young and defend the nest against predators and other birds.
value.dietFeeding: The species has a highly varied diet. It sallies from exposed perches to seize beetles, grasshoppers, dragonflies, and other flying insects, and also gleans prey from vegetation or the ground. It takes spiders, millipedes, lizards, frogs, small snakes, mice, and occasionally nestlings. Near water, it may plunge or hover to capture small fish, tadpoles, frogs, or aquatic invertebrates. Fruits, berries, seeds, and food provided by people are also eaten.
value.behavior: Great Kiskadees are conspicuous, vocal, and assertive. They commonly perch on prominent branches, wires, fences, or poles while surveying open areas and water. Pairs or territory holders may chase raptors, snakes, monkeys, and other potential nest predators. Their flexible foraging behavior allows them to exploit gardens, farms, wetlands, and urban habitats. They often call repeatedly throughout the day, especially while defending territories or communicating with a mate.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable.
